hero.text: Discussion: discuss both views. The question, a plan, the essay itself, and why it would score well.

blocks.title: Unofficial original RCF practice material
text: Original question and essay written by RCF English. Not endorsed by the British Council, IDP: IELTS Australia or Cambridge University Press & Assessment.

blocks.heading: The question
text: *Some people believe that longer prison sentences are the best way to reduce crime. Others argue that education and rehabilitation work better.*
**Discuss both views and give your own opinion.**
*Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.*
*Write at least 250 words.*

blocks.heading: The plan
rows: Rephrase both views in one sentence each. Position: **rehabilitation for most offenders**, prison for the dangerous few.
The case for long sentences, put fairly: deterrence, and public safety while the person is inside.
The case for rehabilitation: reoffending rates, literacy and job training, cost per prisoner.
Where the two meet: violent offenders need prison; most offenders are not violent.
Restate the position with the qualification intact.

items.label: Original RCF model answer (276 words)
items.prompt: Some people believe that longer prison sentences are the best way to reduce crime. Others argue that education and rehabilitation work better. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
sample: People disagree about how to bring crime down. Some want longer prison sentences, while others believe that education and rehabilitation are more effective. In my view, rehabilitation is the better choice for most offenders, though prison remains necessary for a small number.

The argument for long sentences is easy to understand. A person who is in prison cannot commit crimes against the public, and the fear of many years inside may stop some people from offending at all. Victims also feel that a serious crime deserves a serious punishment, and a justice system that ignores this loses public support.

The argument for rehabilitation, however, rests on what happens afterwards. Almost every prisoner is released one day, and the question is what kind of person walks out. Someone who has learnt to read, finished a qualification or trained in a trade has a reason not to return to crime. Someone who has spent ten years with nothing to do has none. Prison is also expensive, and money spent on teaching is usually cheaper than money spent on locking people up for longer.

My own view is that these approaches suit different offenders. A person who is violent and likely to remain so must be kept away from the public, and no training course changes that. Most offenders, though, are not in that group: they are young, poorly educated and often addicted to something. For them, a long sentence teaches nothing and costs a great deal.

In conclusion, prison is necessary for dangerous offenders, but for the majority, education and rehabilitation offer a better return for society, because they reduce the chance that the same person offends again.

items.term: In my view, X is the better choice for most Y, though Z remains necessary for a small number.
items.def: A position with a limit built into it. It answers the question and leaves room for the other side.

items.term: The argument for X is easy to understand.
items.def: A fair, unfussy way to open the side you do not fully support.

items.term: The argument for X, however, rests on what happens afterwards.
items.def: Pivots to your own side and tells the reader what the paragraph will argue.

items.term: My own view is that these approaches suit different X.
items.def: Useful when the honest answer is *it depends*: it keeps a clear position.

items.term: ...because they reduce the chance that the same person offends again.
items.def: A conclusion that gives the reason, not just the verdict.

blocks.heading: Why this would score well
intro: The four things an examiner marks, and what this essay does about each. The wording of the criteria is IELTS's own and is published for candidates; the comments are ours.
rows: Both views are given real weight before the opinion is stated, and the opinion appears in the introduction and again at the end.
One idea to a paragraph, linked by plain words: *however*, *also*, *though*. No list of connectives for their own sake.
Ordinary words used precisely: *deterrence*, *reoffending*, *qualification*. Nothing rare and nothing forced.
A mix of short and long sentences, with relative and conditional clauses used where they fit naturally.

blocks.heading: Check your own attempt
items: Did you give both views before your own, and give the weaker one a fair hearing?
Is your opinion in the introduction as well as the conclusion?
Does each body paragraph make one point, not two half-points?
Did you avoid inventing statistics?
Is your conclusion the reason, not a repeat of the introduction?
Are you between 250 and 300 words?

hero.text: Opinion: to what extent do you agree?. The question, a plan, the essay itself, and why it would score well.

blocks.title: Unofficial original RCF practice material
text: Original question and essay written by RCF English. Not endorsed by the British Council, IDP: IELTS Australia or Cambridge University Press & Assessment.

blocks.heading: The question
text: *Some people think that advertising aimed at children should be banned.*
**To what extent do you agree or disagree?**
*Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.*
*Write at least 250 words.*

blocks.heading: The plan
rows: Rephrase the proposal. Position: **agree for young children**, regulate rather than ban for older ones.
Why young children are a special case: they cannot tell an advertisement from a programme.
What the advertising actually promotes, and the pressure it puts on families.
Why a total ban on all children's advertising goes too far: older children, and free content.
A ban below a certain age, strict rules above it.

items.label: Original RCF model answer (261 words)
items.prompt: Some people think that advertising aimed at children should be banned. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
sample: It is often argued that children should not be advertised to at all. I agree with this where young children are concerned, but I believe regulation is a better answer for older ones.

The case for protecting young children is strong. Below about seven, a child does not reliably understand that an advertisement is trying to sell something. To that child, a cheerful film about a sugary drink is simply part of the programme, and the usual defence of advertising, that adults can judge it for themselves, does not apply. Selling to someone who cannot recognise that they are being sold to is difficult to justify.

There is also the question of what is advertised. Food high in sugar and salt, and toys far beyond what many families can afford, make up a large share of it. The result is pressure inside the home: children ask, parents refuse, and the argument that follows is one the advertiser never has to witness. Poorer families feel this most sharply.

A complete ban, however, would be clumsy. A fifteen-year-old can recognise persuasion and will meet far more of it as an adult; shielding them entirely prepares them for nothing. Much of the free content young people use is paid for by advertising, and removing it would simply move the cost to families.

In conclusion, I support banning advertisements directed at young children, who cannot understand what is being done to them. For older children, strict rules on what may be advertised, combined with teaching them how persuasion works, would achieve more than a ban.

items.term: I agree with this where X is concerned, but I believe Y is a better answer for Z.
items.def: A precise answer to *to what extent*: agreement with a stated boundary.

items.term: The usual defence of X, that ..., does not apply.
items.def: Names the opposing argument and disposes of it in one sentence.

items.term: Selling to someone who cannot recognise that they are being sold to is difficult to justify.
items.def: A sentence that argues rather than asserts. The reason is inside it.

items.term: A complete ban, however, would be clumsy.
items.def: A short pivot sentence. Short sentences carry weight when the others are long.

items.term: ...would achieve more than a ban.
items.def: Ends with a comparison, which is stronger than ending with a repetition.

blocks.heading: Why this would score well
intro: The four things an examiner marks, and what this essay does about each. The wording of the criteria is IELTS's own and is published for candidates; the comments are ours.
rows: *To what extent* is answered with an actual extent: yes below an age, no above it, with reasons for the line.
The paragraphs move from the strongest ground, to a second reason, to the limit of the argument.
Topic words used naturally: *persuasion*, *regulation*, *directed at*. The register stays even.
Relative clauses and a conditional (*would be clumsy*, *would simply move*) used for hypothetical results.

blocks.heading: Check your own attempt
items: Did you say how far you agree, rather than only that you agree?
Did you give the other side a real argument, not a weak one chosen to knock down?
Does your position stay the same from the introduction to the conclusion?
Did you avoid inventing percentages?
Are your examples general rather than about your own family?
Are you between 250 and 300 words?

hero.text: Advantages and disadvantages: do the advantages outweigh them?. The question, a plan, the essay itself, and why it would score well.

blocks.title: Unofficial original RCF practice material
text: Original question and essay written by RCF English. Not endorsed by the British Council, IDP: IELTS Australia or Cambridge University Press & Assessment.

blocks.heading: The question
text: *More and more people are choosing to study online rather than in a classroom.*
**Do the advantages of this development outweigh the disadvantages?**
*Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.*
*Write at least 250 words.*

blocks.heading: The plan
rows: Rephrase the trend. Position: **advantages outweigh**, for adults and for those far from a campus.
The advantages: reach, cost, and studying while working.
The disadvantages, put honestly: dropping out, no classmates, and subjects that need a laboratory.
Why the balance still favours online study: something is better than nothing.
The verdict, with the group it does not suit named.

items.label: Original RCF model answer (272 words)
items.prompt: More and more people are choosing to study online rather than in a classroom. Do the advantages of this development outweigh the disadvantages?
sample: Studying online has grown quickly, and many people now take a course without entering a classroom. In my opinion the benefits of this change are greater than the drawbacks, although it does not suit every student or every subject.

The main advantage is reach. A student in a small town can take a course from a university hundreds of kilometres away, at a fraction of the cost of moving there. Online courses are usually cheaper to run and therefore cheaper to buy, and recorded lessons can be watched late at night, which matters enormously to people who study after work. For an adult with a job and a family, this is often the difference between studying and not studying at all.

The disadvantages are real, however. Far more students begin online courses than finish them, because nobody notices when they quietly stop. A classroom supplies pressure and company: classmates to compare notes with, and a teacher who sees confusion on a face and explains again. Some subjects also resist the format entirely, since a nurse or an engineer cannot be trained through a screen alone.

Even so, the comparison is not between online study and perfect classroom study. For most people choosing an online course, the realistic alternative is no course at all, because the campus is too far, too expensive, or open only at hours they are working. Compared with that, a course finished slowly at home is a clear gain.
In conclusion, online study has genuine weaknesses, particularly for practical subjects and for students who need supervision, but for the many adults it reaches, the advantages are the greater ones.

items.term: In my opinion the benefits of this change are greater than the drawbacks, although it does not suit every X.
items.def: Answers *do the advantages outweigh* directly, with a limit.

items.term: ...which matters enormously to people who study after work.
items.def: Adds who benefits. An advantage is stronger when it has a person attached.

items.term: The disadvantages are real, however.
items.def: Signals the turn honestly. Examiners reward a fair treatment of the other side.

items.term: The comparison is not between X and perfect Y.
items.def: A reframing sentence. This is the kind of thinking that lifts an essay.

items.term: Compared with that, X is a clear gain.
items.def: Draws the conclusion from the comparison you have just set up.

blocks.heading: Why this would score well
intro: The four things an examiner marks, and what this essay does about each. The wording of the criteria is IELTS's own and is published for candidates; the comments are ours.
rows: Both sides are covered and a verdict is given. The final paragraph names who the format does not suit.
Advantages, disadvantages, then the comparison that decides between them: a shape the reader can follow.
Precise ordinary language: *reach*, *supervision*, *resist the format*. No memorised phrases.
Comparatives carry the argument (*greater than*, *far more ... than*), used accurately throughout.

blocks.heading: Check your own attempt
items: Did you actually give a verdict, or only list both sides?
Are your advantages and disadvantages different points, not the same point reversed?
Did you say who the disadvantage affects most?
Did you avoid inventing figures for drop-out rates?
Is the conclusion a judgement rather than a summary?
Are you between 250 and 300 words?

hero.text: Problem and solution: causes and what should be done. The question, a plan, the essay itself, and why it would score well.

blocks.title: Unofficial original RCF practice material
text: Original question and essay written by RCF English. Not endorsed by the British Council, IDP: IELTS Australia or Cambridge University Press & Assessment.

blocks.heading: The question
text: *In many countries people are eating more unhealthy food, and rates of diet-related illness are rising.*
**What are the causes of this, and what measures could governments take to address it?**
*Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.*
*Write at least 250 words.*

blocks.heading: The plan
rows: Rephrase the problem. Signal: two causes, then two measures.
Causes: price and time. Processed food is cheap and instant; fresh food is neither.
Cause: advertising and availability, especially near schools.
Measures: pricing (tax on sugar, support for fresh produce) and rules on advertising and labelling.
Name the measure most likely to work, and why.

items.label: Original RCF model answer (279 words)
items.prompt: In many countries people are eating more unhealthy food, and rates of diet-related illness are rising. What are the causes of this, and what measures could governments take to address it?
sample: Diets in many countries have worsened, and illnesses linked to food, such as diabetes and heart disease, have become more common. This essay will consider the main causes and the steps governments could take.

The first cause is economic. Processed food is usually cheaper per meal than fresh ingredients, keeps for weeks rather than days, and requires no preparation. A parent finishing a shift at eight in the evening is choosing not between healthy and unhealthy food but between food that takes forty minutes and food that takes four. Until that difference in cost and time closes, advice about balanced diets will have limited effect.

The second cause is how heavily this food is promoted and how easily it is found. Advertising for it is constant, and outlets cluster around schools, stations and hospitals. Healthy options, by contrast, are often absent in exactly the places where people are hungry and in a hurry.

Governments can act on both. Pricing is the most direct lever: taxing sugary drinks raises their price and has reduced sales where it has been tried, while subsidies or vouchers can lower the price of vegetables and fruit for low-income households. Rules are the second lever, covering where fast-food outlets may open, what may be advertised to children, and how clearly sugar and salt must be shown on the front of a package, so that a shopper can compare two products in seconds.

In conclusion, unhealthy eating is driven by cost, time and heavy promotion rather than by ignorance. For that reason, measures that change the price and availability of food are likely to achieve more than campaigns that simply tell people what they already know.

items.term: This essay will consider the main causes and the steps X could take.
items.def: A plain signal of structure. It costs one sentence and guides the whole essay.

items.term: A parent ... is choosing not between X and Y but between A and B.
items.def: Reframes the problem. This kind of sentence shows real thought.

items.term: Until that difference closes, advice about X will have limited effect.
items.def: Links cause to solution before you reach the solutions.

items.term: Pricing is the most direct lever.
items.def: Names the tool. *Lever*, *measure*, *step* are useful, plain words here.

items.term: ...are likely to achieve more than campaigns that simply tell people what they already know.
items.def: A conclusion that chooses between the solutions rather than listing them again.

blocks.heading: Why this would score well
intro: The four things an examiner marks, and what this essay does about each. The wording of the criteria is IELTS's own and is published for candidates; the comments are ours.
rows: Both halves of the question are answered, and the measures address the causes actually given, rather than arriving from nowhere.
Causes then measures, with the link between them stated before the change of direction.
The vocabulary of policy used plainly: *subsidies*, *labelling*, *availability*, *outlets*.
Longer sentences with subordinate clauses, kept readable because each one carries a single idea.

blocks.heading: Check your own attempt
items: Did you answer both parts, causes and measures?
Does each measure deal with a cause you actually named?
Did you avoid inventing statistics about illness?
Are your measures specific enough to picture (a tax, a label, a rule on where shops open)?
Does the conclusion choose, rather than repeat?
Are you between 250 and 300 words?

text: Original question and essay written by RCF English. Not endorsed by the British Council, IDP: IELTS Australia or Cambridge University Press & Assessment.

blocks.heading: The question
text: *Some people believe that the spread of global brands and media is destroying local cultures. Others think it increases choice and understanding between countries.*
**Discuss both views and give your own opinion.**
*Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.*
*Write at least 250 words.*

blocks.heading: The plan
rows: Rephrase both views. Position: **the loss is real but uneven**; the gain is real too.
The case for harm: shops, films and food that look the same everywhere; languages and crafts under pressure.
The case for benefit: access to other cultures, and young people choosing rather than being forced.
What decides which happens: whether local culture is supported, taught and profitable.
Position restated: the outcome is a choice, not a fate.

items.label: Original RCF model answer (285 words)
items.prompt: Some people believe that the spread of global brands and media is destroying local cultures. Others think it increases choice and understanding between countries. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
sample: As global companies and media reach further, some argue that local cultures are being erased, while others believe the exchange brings choice and understanding. In my view both effects are genuine, and which one dominates depends on what a country does about it.

The concern about loss is not imagined. Shopping streets in distant cities now hold the same shops, cinemas show the same few films, and children in many places know foreign characters better than the stories of their own region. Languages with small numbers of speakers lose young speakers first, and crafts stop being practised once the people who buy them prefer imported goods. Once these things go, they rarely come back.

The other side, however, is equally true. A person today can read the literature, hear the music and follow the news of countries they will never visit, and that access was impossible for their grandparents. Contact of this kind makes other people harder to caricature. It is also worth remembering that young people are not passive: when they choose foreign music, they are choosing, and calling that destruction is a little insulting to them.

What seems to decide the outcome is whether local culture is actively supported. Where a language is taught in schools, where local films and music are funded, and where traditional work earns a living, both can exist together; the same young person listens to international music and speaks their own language at home. Where nothing is done, the imported version simply fills the space.
In conclusion, global media brings genuine benefits, but a culture survives only if it is taught, funded and used. The loss people fear is a result of neglect rather than an unavoidable consequence.

items.term: ...and which one dominates depends on what a country does about it.
items.def: A position that explains itself. It also sets up the third body paragraph.

items.term: The concern about loss is not imagined.
items.def: Grants the other side seriously in four words.

items.term: Once these things go, they rarely come back.
items.def: A short sentence after long ones. It lands.

items.term: It is also worth remembering that young people are not passive.
items.def: Introduces a point the reader may not have considered.

items.term: The loss people fear is a result of neglect rather than an unavoidable consequence.
items.def: Ends on a distinction, which is a strong way to finish a discussion essay.

blocks.heading: Why this would score well
intro: The four things an examiner marks, and what this essay does about each. The wording of the criteria is IELTS's own and is published for candidates; the comments are ours.
rows: Both views are argued properly, and the opinion is a real third position rather than a repeat of one side.
View, counter-view, then the condition that decides between them. Each paragraph has one job.
Careful, plain choices: *erased*, *caricature*, *neglect*, *passive*. No thesaurus words.
Sentence length varies deliberately, with *where ...* clauses used to set conditions.

blocks.heading: Check your own attempt
items: Did you argue both views before giving your own?
Is your opinion more than agreeing with one side?
Did you avoid naming real companies unnecessarily?
Does every paragraph have one clear job?
Did you vary sentence length on purpose?
Are you between 250 and 300 words?

hero.text: Opinion: to what extent do you agree?. The question, a plan, the essay itself, and why it would score well.

blocks.title: Unofficial original RCF practice material
text: Original question and essay written by RCF English. Not endorsed by the British Council, IDP: IELTS Australia or Cambridge University Press & Assessment.

blocks.heading: The question
text: *Some people think that governments should spend less money on sports facilities and more on health care and education.*
**To what extent do you agree or disagree?**
*Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.*
*Write at least 250 words.*

blocks.heading: The plan
rows: Rephrase the claim. Position: **agree about elite sport**, disagree about ordinary facilities.
Where the claim is right: stadiums and international events, and what that money could do instead.
Where it is wrong: swimming pools and playing fields are health spending under another name.
The distinction that matters: who uses the facility.
Cut the spectacle, keep the pool.

items.label: Original RCF model answer (267 words)
items.prompt: Some people think that governments should spend less money on sports facilities and more on health care and education. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
sample: It is sometimes argued that money spent on sport would be better spent on hospitals and schools. I agree in the case of large-scale, professional sport, but I disagree where ordinary local facilities are concerned.

The argument is strongest against spectacle. Hosting an international tournament or building a stadium for a professional club costs an enormous sum, and the promised benefits, such as tourism and national pride, are hard to measure and often short-lived. The same money would buy equipment for hospitals or pay teachers for years, and those benefits are neither hard to measure nor temporary. Several cities have been left with arenas that are expensive to maintain and rarely full.

Local facilities, however, are a different matter. A public swimming pool, a running track or a playing field costs a small fraction of a stadium and is used every week by ordinary people. Exercise of this kind prevents precisely the illnesses that later fill hospital beds, which means that spending on it is a form of health spending, simply paid earlier. Cutting it to fund hospitals would increase the demand on those hospitals in time.

The useful question, then, is not sport or health, but who uses the facility. If a few professionals use it and the public watches, its value is entertainment. If hundreds of local residents use it every week, its value is health.

In conclusion, I agree that governments should spend less on elite sport, where the returns are uncertain, but the small local facilities that keep ordinary people active deserve protection, because cutting them makes the health budget larger, not smaller.

items.term: I agree in the case of X, but I disagree where Y is concerned.
items.def: A split answer, which is often the honest one. Say which is which immediately.

items.term: The argument is strongest against X.
items.def: Shows you can judge the argument, not merely repeat it.

items.term: ...which means that spending on it is a form of health spending, simply paid earlier.
items.def: Connects the two halves of the question instead of treating them separately.

items.term: The useful question, then, is not X or Y, but ...
items.def: Reframing. It signals to the examiner that you are thinking, not listing.

items.term: ...because cutting them makes the health budget larger, not smaller.
items.def: A conclusion with a reason that bites.

blocks.heading: Why this would score well
intro: The four things an examiner marks, and what this essay does about each. The wording of the criteria is IELTS's own and is published for candidates; the comments are ours.
rows: The extent is exact: agreement for elite sport, disagreement for local facilities, with a test for telling them apart.
Concede, counter, then supply the distinction. The reader always knows which side a paragraph is on.
Plain but exact: *spectacle*, *arenas*, *returns*, *facilities*. Repetition is avoided by meaning, not by synonyms.
Conditionals set up the test (*If a few professionals use it ...*), and are accurate.

blocks.heading: Check your own attempt
items: Did you give an extent rather than a flat yes or no?
Did you distinguish between types of sports spending?
Does your conclusion add a reason rather than repeat the introduction?
Did you avoid inventing costs and figures?
Are your examples general rather than about one named event?
Are you between 250 and 300 words?

hero.text: Problem and solution: problems and what should be done. The question, a plan, the essay itself, and why it would score well.

blocks.title: Unofficial original RCF practice material
text: Original question and essay written by RCF English. Not endorsed by the British Council, IDP: IELTS Australia or Cambridge University Press & Assessment.

blocks.heading: The question
text: *In many countries people are working longer hours than in the past.*
**What problems does this cause, and what can be done to solve them?**
*Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.*
*Write at least 250 words.*

blocks.heading: The plan
rows: Rephrase the trend. Signal: problems for health and family, then two kinds of solution.
Problems: health, and the work that gets worse as hours get longer.
Problems at home: children, and unpaid work falling on one person.
Solutions: legal limits and the right to disconnect; employers measuring output rather than hours.
Which solution has to come first, and why.

items.label: Original RCF model answer (266 words)
items.prompt: In many countries people are working longer hours than in the past. What problems does this cause, and what can be done to solve them?
sample: Working hours have lengthened in many countries, helped by phones that make employees reachable at any time. This essay will outline the main problems this creates and suggest how they could be reduced.

The first problem is health. People who work very long weeks sleep less, exercise less and eat worse, and stress-related illness follows. There is also a problem for the employer, although it is less obvious: after a certain number of hours the quality of the work falls, mistakes increase, and the extra time produces little of value. Long hours and productive hours are not the same thing.

The second problem is at home. A parent who leaves before their children wake and returns after they sleep is present in the household but absent from it. Within couples, the housework and childcare usually fall to whichever partner works fewer paid hours, which is a common reason why one career advances and the other stalls.

Two kinds of solution would help. The first is legal: a maximum working week, enforced with real penalties, and a right to ignore messages outside working hours, as several countries have now introduced. The second is a change in how employers judge staff. Where managers measure hours in the office, employees stay late to be seen; where they measure work completed, staying late has no purpose.

In conclusion, long hours damage health, family life and often the work itself. Legal limits are the necessary first step, because individual employees cannot negotiate this alone, but lasting change also requires employers to stop treating time at a desk as evidence of effort.

items.term: This essay will outline the main problems and suggest how they could be reduced.
items.def: One sentence of signposting. Enough.

items.term: Long hours and productive hours are not the same thing.
items.def: A short sentence that states the insight plainly.

items.term: ...is present in the household but absent from it.
items.def: A contrast in six words. Worth more than an elaborate phrase.

items.term: Where managers measure X, employees do Y; where they measure Z, ...
items.def: A parallel structure showing cause and effect on both sides.

items.term: ...because individual employees cannot negotiate this alone.
items.def: Explains why one solution must come first. Ranking solutions shows judgement.

blocks.heading: Why this would score well
intro: The four things an examiner marks, and what this essay does about each. The wording of the criteria is IELTS's own and is published for candidates; the comments are ours.
rows: Problems and solutions are both developed, and the solutions match the problems described.
Two problems, two solutions, then a ranking. Nothing is left for the reader to assemble.
Parallel *where ...* clauses and relative clauses, controlled rather than decorative.

blocks.heading: Check your own attempt
items: Did you answer both parts, problems and solutions?
Is each solution connected to a problem you named?
Did you include a problem the reader might not expect?
Did you avoid inventing statistics about working hours?
Does the conclusion say which solution matters most?
Are you between 250 and 300 words?

blocks.title: Unofficial original RCF practice material
text: Original question and essay written by RCF English. Not endorsed by the British Council, IDP: IELTS Australia or Cambridge University Press & Assessment.

blocks.heading: The question
text: *Some people believe schools should concentrate on science and technology, because these subjects are most useful to a country's economy. Others believe the arts are equally important.*
**Discuss both views and give your own opinion.**
*Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.*
*Write at least 250 words.*

blocks.heading: The plan
rows: Rephrase both views. Position: **a false choice**; the school years are for breadth.
The case for science: jobs, national development, and where the shortages are.
The case for the arts: judgement, expression, and the industries the arts support.
Why a school is the wrong place to specialise: children choose at fifteen with poor information.

items.label: Original RCF model answer (257 words)
items.prompt: Some people believe schools should concentrate on science and technology, because these subjects are most useful to a country's economy. Others believe the arts are equally important. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
sample: There is a long-running argument about whether schools should prioritise science and technology or give the arts equal weight. In my view the choice is a false one, at least while pupils are still at school.

The case for science is practical. Countries need engineers, doctors and technicians, shortages in these fields are real, and the qualifications lead reliably to employment. A government paying for education can reasonably ask what the country gets in return, and scientific training produces an answer that is easy to see.

The case for the arts is easy to state badly, so it is worth stating properly. Studying literature, history or music teaches a pupil to interpret, to judge evidence and to express an idea so that another person understands it, and those abilities are needed in any career, including scientific ones. The arts also underpin industries that employ large numbers of people, from design and publishing to film, which are rarely counted when the economic argument is made.

My own view rests on the age of the pupils. A child of fifteen choosing between these paths knows very little about either, and a school system that forces the choice early will lose good scientists who were never taught properly and good writers who were told the subject was worthless. Specialisation belongs at university, when the student knows more.

In conclusion, science and the arts are both necessary, and the sensible arrangement is breadth at school followed by depth afterwards. A country that neglects either ends up short of something it needs.

items.term: In my view the choice is a false one, at least while ...
items.def: Rejects the premise, which is a legitimate and strong position if you justify it.

items.term: The case for X is easy to state badly, so it is worth stating properly.
items.def: Signals that you know the weak version of the argument and will not use it.

items.term: ...which are rarely counted when the economic argument is made.
items.def: Answers the other side's strongest point on its own terms.

items.term: My own view rests on the age of the pupils.
items.def: Tells the reader exactly what your opinion depends on.

items.term: A country that neglects either ends up short of something it needs.
items.def: A final sentence that is general without being empty.

blocks.heading: Why this would score well
intro: The four things an examiner marks, and what this essay does about each. The wording of the criteria is IELTS's own and is published for candidates; the comments are ours.
rows: Both views are argued, and the opinion is a genuine third position with a stated basis.
Each paragraph announces its job in its first sentence, so the essay can be followed at speed.
Relative clauses carry the extra information, and the long sentences stay grammatical.

blocks.heading: Check your own attempt
items: Did you argue both sides before giving your opinion?
If you rejected the premise, did you justify why?
Did you answer the other side's strongest point, not its weakest?
Did you avoid inventing employment figures?
Is the conclusion a judgement rather than a summary?
Are you between 250 and 300 words?

hero.text: Two-part question. The question, a plan, the essay itself, and why it would score well.

blocks.title: Unofficial original RCF practice material
text: Original question and essay written by RCF English. Not endorsed by the British Council, IDP: IELTS Australia or Cambridge University Press & Assessment.

blocks.heading: The question
text: *People now share a great deal of personal information on social media.*
**Why do they do this, and should governments regulate what is shared?**
*Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.*
*Write at least 250 words.*

blocks.heading: The plan
rows: Rephrase both parts. Signal: reasons first, then a qualified yes on regulation.
Why people share: connection, and the design of the platforms themselves.
Why people underestimate the risk: the audience feels small.
Regulation: yes for how companies use the data, no for what adults choose to post.
Regulate the company, teach the user.

items.label: Original RCF model answer (280 words)
items.prompt: People now share a great deal of personal information on social media. Why do they do this, and should governments regulate what is shared?
sample: Social media users publish a great deal about themselves, from holidays to opinions to the details of their children's lives. This essay will consider why this happens and whether governments should intervene.

The first reason is straightforward: people are sociable, and sharing news is what friends have always done. What has changed is the design of the platforms. They are built to reward posting, with likes and comments arriving within seconds, and that immediate response encourages people to post again. Many users also maintain a version of themselves online, and a version needs material.

A second reason is that the risk feels smaller than it is. Writing a post feels like speaking to a few friends, because the replies come from friends, and it is easy to forget that the audience is far larger and that the record is permanent. Information that seems harmless alone, such as a school name and a daily routine, becomes useful to a stranger once it is combined.

On regulation, I would distinguish between two things. What an adult chooses to publish is their own business, and a government deciding what may be posted is a serious step towards censorship. How companies collect, store, combine and sell that information is a different question entirely, and there the user has no real choice, since refusing the terms means not using the service. Rules there, including strict protection for children's accounts, are justified.

In conclusion, people share because it is sociable and because the platforms are designed to encourage it, and they underestimate how public it is. Governments should regulate the companies rather than the users, and schools should teach young people what a permanent record means.

items.term: This essay will consider why this happens and whether X should intervene.
items.def: Names both parts of a two-part question in one sentence.

items.term: What has changed is the design of the platforms.
items.def: A *what*-clause used for emphasis. Simple and effective.

items.term: ...it is easy to forget that the audience is far larger and that the record is permanent.
items.def: Two parallel *that*-clauses: tidy and accurate.

items.term: On X, I would distinguish between two things.
items.def: Announces that your answer has two parts, so the reader follows the split.

items.term: Governments should regulate the companies rather than the users.
items.def: A conclusion in one line that anyone could quote back.

blocks.heading: Why this would score well
intro: The four things an examiner marks, and what this essay does about each. The wording of the criteria is IELTS's own and is published for candidates; the comments are ours.
rows: Both questions are answered separately and fully, and the second answer is qualified rather than a flat yes or no.
Reason, second reason, then the two halves of the regulation answer. The structure mirrors the question.
Precise words for an abstract topic: *censorship*, *permanent record*, *terms*, *intervene*.
Noun clauses and comparatives handled cleanly; the longer sentences do not lose control.

blocks.heading: Check your own attempt
items: Did you answer both questions, and give each a fair share of the essay?
Is your answer on regulation specific about what would be regulated?
Did you avoid naming particular companies unnecessarily?
Did you avoid inventing figures about users?
Does your conclusion answer both parts?
Are you between 250 and 300 words?

hero.text: Two-part question. The question, a plan, the essay itself, and why it would score well.

blocks.title: Unofficial original RCF practice material
text: Original question and essay written by RCF English. Not endorsed by the British Council, IDP: IELTS Australia or Cambridge University Press & Assessment.

blocks.heading: The question
text: *Many people believe that individuals can do little about climate change and that only governments and large companies can make a difference.*
**To what extent do you agree, and what could ordinary people do?**
*Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.*
*Write at least 250 words.*

blocks.heading: The plan
rows: Rephrase the claim. Position: **largely agree on scale**, but individuals matter in two particular ways.
Why the claim is largely right: where the emissions actually come from.
Where individuals still count: voting and demand, which change what governments and companies do.
What ordinary people can do, concretely: travel, heating, food, and pressure.
Both, with the causal link between them stated.

items.label: Original RCF model answer (272 words)
items.prompt: Many people believe that individuals can do little about climate change and that only governments and large companies can make a difference. To what extent do you agree, and what could ordinary people do?
sample: It is often said that climate change is too large for individuals to affect, and that governments and corporations must act instead. I largely agree with the first part, but I think it underestimates two things individuals do that matter a great deal.

The scale argument is sound. Most emissions come from electricity generation, heavy industry, agriculture and transport systems, and no household decision reaches them. A family that recycles carefully has changed almost nothing about how its country produces power. Told that personal effort is the answer, many people reasonably conclude that the problem is hopeless, and this is why the claim is usually right.

It is incomplete, however, because governments and companies respond to people. Governments that act on climate are elected by voters who wanted it, and policies survive only while that support lasts. Companies, similarly, follow demand: when enough customers change what they buy, the product changes, and the change reaches the factory. Individuals therefore act less as consumers than as citizens.

In practical terms, this suggests what is worth doing. The decisions with real weight are the large and infrequent ones: how a home is heated and insulated, whether a car is needed at all, how often one flies, and how much meat is eaten. Alongside these, people can vote on the issue, ask their employer about its energy use, and support organisations that hold companies to their promises.

In conclusion, the claim is right about scale and wrong about influence. Governments and industry must make the large changes, but they make them because enough ordinary people, acting as voters and customers, made it costly not to.

items.term: I largely agree with the first part, but I think it underestimates ...
items.def: Answers *to what extent* and announces what the rest of the essay will add.

items.term: The scale argument is sound.
items.def: Concedes in four words so the paragraph can spend its length on evidence.

items.term: It is incomplete, however, because ...
items.def: The pivot. *Incomplete* is more precise than *wrong* and more honest.

items.term: Individuals therefore act less as consumers than as citizens.
items.def: A *less as X than as Y* comparison, which is a neat structure to have ready.

items.term: ...made it costly not to.
items.def: A short, concrete ending after an abstract argument.

blocks.heading: Why this would score well
intro: The four things an examiner marks, and what this essay does about each. The wording of the criteria is IELTS's own and is published for candidates; the comments are ours.
rows: The extent is stated and both parts are answered; the practical suggestions follow from the argument rather than being a list.
Concede, qualify, then apply. The final paragraph ties the two halves together.
Accurate topic language: *emissions*, *insulated*, *demand*, *generation*, without slipping into jargon.
Participle openings and comparative structures used correctly, with clean punctuation in long sentences.

blocks.heading: Check your own attempt
items: Did you state how far you agree, and answer the second question too?
Are your suggestions the ones that actually matter, rather than the easiest to list?
Did you connect individual action to government and company action?
Did you avoid inventing percentages for emissions?
Does the conclusion answer both parts in one movement?
Are you between 250 and 300 words?
